Observable inventory streaming with Confluent and Datadog #

Follow this workshop on its website: https://gianlucanatali.github.io/observable-inventory-streaming/workshop.html. There you choose the control panel or the terminal once and see only the steps for your choice, with copy buttons and term explanations. This Markdown file is the source of that page and shows both paths.

UrbanStreet, a fictional outdoor retailer, has five shoe stores in Italy and an Online shop. The Online shop must show how many pairs are left across all five stores. Then a new release makes it slow. In this workshop you build the whole path yourself, with PostgreSQL, Debezium, Confluent Cloud and Redis on AWS. Then you use Datadog to find the cause of the slowdown and roll out a fix safely.

Every product, store, sale and shopper in this workshop is synthetic.

The idea in three boxes

The store databases keep selling as they always did. Their changes flow through Confluent Cloud, and the Online shop reads only the copy. Datadog shows whether each part is healthy. Everything else in this workshop is a closer look at one of these boxes.

Which layers each Chapter needs #

You choose one of two ways. Both build the same stack. The difference is when the optional layers start billing.

  • Step by step (default, cheaper). Write layers: core in demo.yaml, or leave the layers: key out: no key means core only. Each Lab that needs a new layer begins with a "Turn on" step, so you pay only for the layers you run. Chapters 1 and 2 are enough to see the main idea.
  • Everything at once. Write layers: all in demo.yaml. Every layer comes up together, so you can look around freely. It bills the full rate from the first minute, about $1.50 to $2.50 per hour (Reference D). Skip every "Turn on" step.
More about layers and their cost

Which Chapter needs which layer, what each one bills, and how to add one.

Chapter Labs Layers needed What the layers add
1. One honest number 1.1, 1.2 (optional) core The five stores, Debezium, Confluent Cloud, Flink, Redis, the stock API and the Online shop, with Datadog on top.
2. Unknown is not zero 2.1 core Nothing new.
3. The incident 3.1 core,releases Releases 1.1.0 (slow) and 1.2.0 (fix), the traffic split and the p95-by-version monitor
4. Canary the fix 4.1 core,releases Nothing new: releases is already on from Chapter 3.
5. The AI offer 5.1, 5.2 (optional) offers for 5.1, restock for 5.2, each turned on by its Lab offers: offers for carts. restock: automatic reordering
6. Datadog on top 6.1 dd-streams, dd-synthetics, dd-rum (keep only the ones you want) Datadog integrations and tests

A stack with every layer is layers: core,releases,restock,offers,dd-streams,dd-synthetics,dd-rum. What each group of layers bills:

  • core: the base of every stack. On AWS that is the VM, the Fargate services, ElastiCache and the load balancer. On Confluent Cloud it is the cluster and one Flink statement.
  • releases: two more small Fargate services, 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB each.
  • restock and offers: restock adds three running Flink statements and a procurement database container on the VM. offers adds one Flink statement and a Fargate service.
  • dd-streams, dd-synthetics, dd-rum: Datadog usage on your trial, plus a small amount of AWS and Confluent for the Confluent integration and the Synthetics private location.

How to add a layer when you build step by step:

  1. In demo.yaml, add the layer to the layers: line. Do this first: make layer-on changes the running stack but not the file, and a later ./demo create applies the file again, which would switch the layer off.
  2. Run make layer-on L=<layer> CONFIRM=yes. Each Lab that needs a layer starts with a "Turn on" step that gives the exact command and what it creates.

What one layer costs. We have no measured cost per layer. The estimate at the top of this page is for a stack with every layer on. A core-only stack costs less, and Reference D lists the billed pieces and their prices, so you can add up your own total. Confluent bills a partial hour as a full hour, so turning a layer on and off within one hour still costs that hour.

The whole picture, for later #

This is the full architecture. You do not need to understand it now: each Chapter shows the part it adds, and Figure 1 is where they all end up.

What you will build
  • Five PostgreSQL store databases, left unchanged. Debezium sends every stock change from them to Confluent Cloud.
  • An online side on AWS that reads stock from Redis and never queries a store. A check compares Redis with the stores.
  • Three releases of the stock lookup service behind a load balancer, plus optional layers for restocking and AI-chosen offers. Datadog monitors all of it.

What you will learn

  • Why streaming the changes out of existing databases lets you avoid replacing those databases, and how to make sure the copy matches them.
  • How a canary catches a slow release while it gets only 10% of traffic, how version tags in Datadog APM show where the slowdown comes from, and how to roll out the fix the same way.
  • How to keep an AI decision optional and explainable.

Conventions. Once you have the code (0.1.4 Get the code), run every command from the root of the repository. Values you must replace look like <this>. Output blocks show what you should see. In an output, <...> is a value that is different on your run, and ... marks lines that were left out.

Two ways to run the labs. You can run every lab step from the control panel, a web page with one button per step, or from the terminal with make commands. Both change the stack in the same way. Pick one path and use it from start to finish: the control panel and the terminal each remember their own last routing for Rollback, so mixing them in one run can roll back to the wrong state. In the Markdown file you see both: steps that differ appear twice, once under With the control panel and once under With the terminal. The workshop website shows only the path you choose.

Two ways through this workshop

  • Step by step. One page per Chapter: Setup, then six Chapters of one or two labs each, with a summary and a checkpoint. Choose your path below, then press Start.

Why change events #

So the stores publish each change as it happens. A change event says that one stock position changed at a Source: which store, which product, the new quantity and its revision, a number that goes up with every change. For example, when the Bologna store sells one pair of the Trailrunner GTX (in the box below).

The Online shop reads a serving view: a copy of the stock positions in Redis that the change stream keeps up to date and can rebuild at any time. Two rules keep the view from showing a wrong number, and you will see both in the labs:

  • A newer revision always wins. An older or repeated event changes nothing, so you can safely replay events.
  • When the view is not sure about a position, the answer is unknown stock, never zero.

A product that does not sell produces no events, so from the outside a quiet product looks the same as a broken feed. A probe solves this: a synthetic stock position that changes every few seconds in each store. If the probe's changes stop reaching the serving view, the feed has stopped. The time a change takes to get from the Source to the serving view is the freshness.

More about this step

The problem: why not just query the stores? Every retailer with physical stores already has stock data. It lives in the store systems that run the checkouts, and nobody wants to rewrite them. In this workshop five PostgreSQL databases play that role, one per store. We call them the Sources. Nothing in this workshop changes how they work.

The Online shop needs sellable stock: the sum of a product's stock across all five stores. If the shop queries all five databases on every page view, shopper traffic lands on the systems the stores use to sell. If you copy the databases once a night instead, the number can be hours old, and the same last pair can be sold twice.

A change event up close: the record, SKUs and how Debezium captures it.

JSON
{ "store_id": "S03", "product_id": "P0042", "quantity": 2, "revision": 1187, "changed_at": "2026-10-04T18:21:57Z" }

The field names are simplified here. The real records are Avro, wrapped in a Debezium envelope.

A product_id such as P0042 is a SKU: one model in one colour and one size. Every part of the path tracks stock per SKU: the stores, the change events, Kafka, Flink, Redis and the stock API. Only the Online shop groups SKUs into models for display (see 0.2.5 Open the shop, the control panel and Datadog).

Change data capture (CDC) turns committed database changes into these events. Here Debezium does it: it reads PostgreSQL's write-ahead log, so the store applications do not change and the store databases get no extra queries. Apache Kafka keeps the events as an ordered log on disk, and each reader reads it at its own pace.

The architecture at a glance #

Figure 1 at the top shows the whole system. It runs in three places, plus Datadog.

The demo is split into layers that you can switch on or off. Core is always on. Each lab adds or uses one layer and shows it in a diagram with the same layout.

A stack is one complete deployment, separate from any other. This guide uses a stack named hybrid. You build it with core only and add the other layers when a lab needs them (Which layers each Chapter needs); the screenshots and examples come from a run with every layer on. The details of each component, connector and signal are in the Reference.

More about this step

What runs where.

Zone What runs there
Simulated store estate: one EC2 VM with Docker Compose The five store databases, a procurement database, a self-managed Kafka Connect worker (Debezium sources and sink connectors), background sales, the freshness probe (freshness-probe), a supplier simulator, the scenario-api that runs the load, verify and canary checks for the control panel, and a Datadog Agent
Confluent Cloud (AWS eu-west-1) One Basic Kafka cluster, Schema Registry and a Flink compute pool running SQL statements
AWS online side (eu-west-1) ECS Fargate services behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB), and an ElastiCache Redis serving view
Datadog (EU site) APM, logs, Data Streams Monitoring, dashboards, monitors, LLM Observability, Synthetics, RUM and cost

Labs #

Lab What happens to the shop What you show
1.1 A product sells out in all five stores The online number follows within seconds, without querying any store
1.2 (optional) The same sale, seen from inside The change event in Confluent Cloud, and its path in Stream Lineage
2.1 One store stops reporting The shop shows "at least" instead of a wrong number, and Datadog names the store
3.1 A new release is slow The canary check stops it at 10% of traffic; APM shows why
4.1 The fix goes out The same check lets it through, step by step, with a way back
5.1 (optional layer) A shopper's product sells out in their cart An offer, chosen by AI only when it is confident enough
5.2 (optional layer) A product runs out The system orders more and the stock comes back
6.1 Nothing breaks Datadog's view of the whole platform: integrations, tests, monitors, cost

Every lab follows the same pattern: start from a clean state with Full demo reset (or make reset; Lab 1.2 and Lab 4 continue from the lab before, and Lab 6 turns background sales on instead), do one thing to the shop, look at the result in the shop and in Datadog, then tick the checkpoint.

Before each lab: the stack name, and where to get help

The labs tell one story about UrbanStreet's Online shop. Do them in order: each lab uses what the one before showed you. They are grouped by the layers they need (Which layers each Chapter needs).

Every lab expects the stack from 0.2 Build the stack to be running and warmed up. On the terminal path, run the commands from the repository root: the make commands read your stack name from demo.yaml. The examples use the stack name hybrid; if you chose another one (the stack name in 0.2.1), read dd-demo-<your name> for the hybrid environment name and stack:<your name> for the hybrid stack tag. Each lab first says what you will do and why, then shows the part of the architecture it uses. If something does not work, see Troubleshooting.
